errors: No mathematical errors. I checked every divisor list exponent-tuple by exponent-tuple. Each list is complete and free of duplicates, and each stated count (4, 6, 8; 5, 8, 9, 12, 16; 6, 10, 12, 16, 18, 24) is correct.

Minor verbal imprecision in §68: the phrase 'prout horum factorum bini, vel tres, vel omnes quatuor fuerint aequales' does not explicitly mention the 'two pairs equal' case (p^2q^2) or the 'none equal' case (pqrs). The actual list of five species is nevertheless complete and correct.

results.what: Classification of integers by Omega(n) (class) and by the exponent pattern of the prime factorization (species). The species in class k correspond to the partitions of k: 2, 3, 5 and 7 species for k = 2, 3, 4, 5.
results.modern_name: Prime signature / partition of Omega(n); number of signatures with Omega = k equals the partition number p(k)
results.usually_credited_to: Folklore; the notion of prime signature is modern terminology

results.what: Complete divisor lists for every prime signature up to Omega = 5, with counts 3, 4; 4, 6, 8; 5, 8, 9, 12, 16; 6, 10, 12, 16, 18, 24, 32.
results.modern_name: Divisor function d(n) = tau(n) = product of (a_i + 1)
results.usually_credited_to: Divisor-count rule known in the 17th century (e.g. van Schooten, Wallis, Prestet)

deep.surprise_reason: This is elementary textbook material from Euler's published (1862) Tractatus. It consists of divisor enumeration by prime signature, leading to the well-known formula d(n) = ∏(a_i + 1), which predates Euler.

checkable.asserts: Number of species per class equals the partition number
Euler's explicit list for p^2q^2r (p=2, q=3, r=5) is exactly the divisor set

transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image. No substantive corrections needed (only a minor typographical variation, 'p, p^2' with a stray comma or point in the p^5 line of §71).
